# Layer-12 role-probe transfer to agentic trajectories

## Motivation & RQ

Do role probes trained on neutral text recognize who is speaking in realistic agent conversations? We test transfer to model-generated histories from two agentic benchmarks.

## Evaluation setup

**Data.** We evaluate GPT-OSS-20B on 114 τ²-bench retail conversations and 500 SWE-bench Verified software-repair attempts. These histories were generated by the evaluated model (on-policy). Both successful and unsuccessful benchmark attempts are included.

**Probe.** We freeze the model and an existing linear classifier: a multinomial logistic-regression probe mapping each token's hidden state to five role probabilities—system, user, reasoning, assistant, and tool. It was trained on neutral C4/Dolma passages placed in each role, not on these agentic datasets; see the [training report](../../role_probes/gptoss20b_baseline/README.md). Here it reads layer 12 activations after attention normalization and before the feed-forward network. The highest-probability role is its prediction. Message roles and reasoning-channel metadata supply ground truth; only message-content tokens are scored.

**Application.** We replay saved conversations in a common chat format, preserving reasoning and tool information. Long histories are processed in separate segments, so later segments lack earlier context. This measures recognition in reconstructed conversations, not the exact activations encountered during generation.

**Metrics and baseline.** Token accuracy is the fraction of content tokens classified correctly; longer conversations contribute more. Mean conversation accuracy first computes accuracy for each conversation and then averages, giving each equal weight. The majority-role baseline always predicts the most frequent true role in that dataset: reasoning for both datasets. Role recall is the fraction of tokens of a particular true role classified correctly.

## Factual observations

| Dataset | Token accuracy | Majority-role baseline | Mean conversation accuracy |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| τ² retail | 29.91% | 83.91% | 31.60% |
| SWE-bench Verified | 26.98% | 46.37% | 28.43% |

Layer 12 falls below the majority-role baseline on both datasets. Tool recall is particularly low: 1.14% on retail and 3.73% on SWE. In retail, 66.8% of reasoning tokens are classified as ordinary assistant output; in SWE, 57.1% of tool tokens are classified as user text.

See [confusion matrices and supplementary metrics](APPENDIX.md), including the effect of giving roles equal weight and results for conversations that fit in one segment. Benchmark task success is reported separately for [retail](../tau2_retail_full/README.md) and [SWE](../swe_bench_full/README.md).

## Message

The layer-12 probe does not reliably transfer from neutral role-labeled text to agentic conversations, especially for tool messages. The [layer comparison](../probe_layer_comparison/README.md) tests whether this weakness depends on which model layer is read.

The datasets differ in tasks, role frequencies, formatting and conversation lengths, so cross-dataset differences cannot be attributed to any one factor. SWE also contains many attempts interrupted by model API failures.
